pages.subheadline: Bayesian Inference for Accelerated Molecular Dynamics Simulations

pages.headline: The Computational Bottleneck in Ab Initio MD
body_points: First-principles calculations provide accuracy but are prohibitively expensive for large-scale or long-time simulations
Traditional force fields lack transferability across different chemical environments
Manual force field development is time-consuming and requires expert knowledge
pages.visual_hints: Split-screen composition showing dense electronic density maps (left) versus expansive empty simulation boxes (right), clock faces superimposed on molecular trajectories indicating time constraints, dark blue gradient background

pages.headline: On-the-Fly MLFF via Bayesian Active Learning
body_points: Bayesian inference enables real-time uncertainty quantification during molecular dynamics
First-principles calculations executed only when encountering configurations outside existing dataset
Automatic dataset construction and force field updates during simulation runtime
pages.visual_hints: Circular workflow diagram showing MD simulation → Uncertainty check → Conditional DFT calculation → Dataset update → MLFF retraining, rendered as glowing pipeline with data flow particles, orange and teal accent colors, dark background

pages.headline: Computational Efficiency Breakthrough
body_points: >99% of first-principles calculations bypassed during force field generation phase
Simulations accelerated by factor of 1000 compared to direct first-principles calculations
Validation performed using thermodynamic perturbation theory ensuring quantitative accuracy
pages.visual_hints: Infographic style with large bold 3D typography for '>99%' and '1000×' floating in space, speedometer or acceleration metaphor, comparison bars showing tiny DFT calculation count versus massive MLFF prediction count, glowing particles, dark teal background with orange highlights

pages.headline: Melting Point Calculations for Five Materials
body_points: Applied to calculate melting points of Aluminum (Al), Silicon (Si), Germanium (Ge), Tin (Sn), and Magnesium Oxide (MgO)
Solid-liquid coexistence simulations performed for all five material systems
Quantitative reproduction of first-principles melting points achieved across metallic and ionic systems
pages.visual_hints: Periodic table highlighting Al, Si, Ge, Sn, Mg, O elements with glowing borders, crystal structure models showing solid-liquid interfaces with thermal gradients (orange to blue), phase coexistence visualization with ordered lattice transitioning to disordered liquid, dark scientific background
facts_to_preserve: Al, Si, Ge, Sn, and MgO

pages.headline: Accuracy Validation via Thermodynamic Perturbation
body_points: Machine learning force fields quantitatively reproduce first-principles melting points
Thermodynamic perturbation theory employed for rigorous accuracy verification
Systematic validation performed across diverse chemical systems including metals and oxides

facts_to_preserve: quantitative reproduction of first-principles melting points

pages.headline: Integration into Electronic-Structure Codes
body_points: Method integrated directly into electronic-structure codes for seamless workflow
Real-time Bayesian active learning occurs during molecular dynamics simulation
Automatic force field updates require no manual intervention or external preprocessing

pages.headline: Transforming Computational Materials Science
body_points: Enables previously intractable materials studies requiring long timescales or large system sizes
Bridges the gap between quantum mechanical accuracy and computational efficiency
Eliminates manual force field development bottleneck for complex chemical environments

pages.headline: Key Achievements
body_points: On-the-fly generation eliminates manual force field development and dataset curation
First-principles calculations bypassed for >99% of configurations during generation phase
1000× acceleration achieved while maintaining quantitative accuracy validated by thermodynamic perturbation theory
Successful application to melting points of Al, Si, Ge, Sn, and MgO
